title: Enhanced and robust superconductivity in La0.8Sr0.2NiO2 membranes compressed up to 210 GPa
authors: Shu Cai, Yuqing Tian, Shengjun Yan, Jinyu Zhao, Bo Hao, Jianfeng Zhang, Shuaihang Sun, Yang Ding, Qi Wu, Ho-kwang Mao, I. Bozovic, Yuefeng Nie, Liling Sun
abstract: The discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelate thin films has opened a new frontier for exploring unconventional oxide superconductors beyond the copper oxide family. However, the presence of substrate hampers investigations under very high pressure. Recently, this problem was circumvented by a study of freestanding Nd0.85Sr0.15NiO2 membranes, which revealed that superconducting transition temperature kept increasing as the pressure was ramped up to 91 GPa, without showing signs of saturation. Naturally, one wonders what would happen at even higher pressures. Here, we report that superconductivity in a freestanding La0.8Sr0.2NiO2 membrane persists under applied ultrahigh pressures up to 210 GPa. The superconducting transition onset temperature exhibits a continuous dome-like evolution, increasing from 16 K at ambient pressure to a peak of 74.5 K at 146 GPa, and then gradually decreasing to 57.4 K at 210 GPa. Such robustness of superconductivity against ultrahigh pressure has not been observed in high-Tc oxide superconductors before.
summary: This work reports on the superconducting behavior of freestanding $	ext{La}_{0.8}	ext{Sr}_{0.2}	ext{NiO}_2$ membranes subjected to ultrahigh pressures up to 210 GPa. The key finding is that superconductivity remains robust, showing a characteristic dome-like increase in transition temperature, peaking at 74.5 K under compression before gradually decreasing. This demonstrates a novel pathway for studying high-$T_c$ superconductivity without substrate constraints.
main_problem: To investigate the enhanced and robust superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelate membranes under extreme high pressures, overcoming substrate limitations.
main_result: Superconductivity persists up to 210 GPa, exhibiting a dome-like evolution where $T_{c	ext{onset}}$ peaks at 74.5 K at 146 GPa before decreasing slightly.
method: High-pressure electrical resistance measurements were performed *in situ* using Diamond Anvil Cells (DAC) on freestanding $	ext{La}_{0.8}	ext{Sr}_{0.2}	ext{NiO}_2$ membranes.
model_or_system: The system is the infinite-layer nickelate superconductor, $	ext{La}_{0.8}	ext{Sr}_{0.2}	ext{NiO}_2$, studied as freestanding membranes to eliminate substrate effects common in high-pressure studies of cuprates and other oxides.
key_observables: Superconducting transition onset temperature ($T_{	ext{conset}}$), critical magnetic field ($\mu_0H_{c2}$), and resistance vs. temperature/pressure curves.
important_parameters: Pressure range up to 210 GPa; peak $T_{c	ext{onset}} = 74.5 	ext{ K}$ at $P = 146 	ext{ GPa}$.
main_assumptions: The superconducting state enhancement is genuine, confirmed by the simultaneous increase in both $T_{	ext{conset}}$ and $\mu_0H_{c2}$ with pressure.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD confirming the infinite-layer phase, zero-field resistance measurements before/after transfer, and multiple panels illustrating the evolution of $T_{	ext{conset}}(P)$ across the entire pressure range.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context by noting the success of nickelates over cuprates. It details sample preparation (membranes) and measurement techniques under DAC compression. The core results present the quantitative dome-like dependence of $T_{	ext{conset}}$ on pressure, culminating in the discussion of robustness up to 210 GPa.
why_interesting: The study provides empirical evidence for superconductivity enhancement far beyond pressures where other high-$T_c$ superconductors fail, offering insights into the fundamental electronic mechanisms governing pairing in nickelates under extreme compression.
